# Consulting

`customer_support.offering.service.consulting` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.service`

> Advice as the deliverable. The client is buying judgement, analysis and recommendation rather than a built artefact, and the structural consequence for support is severe: there is very often no system to break. Most of what a support function does — reproduce, diagnose, fix, verify — assumes a thing that is malfunctioning, and consulting frequently has none. What arrives instead is disagreement. The client disputes a finding, wants the analysis re-run against different assumptions, or believes the recommendation does not fit their situation. That is not a defect and it is not a change request; it is an intellectual disagreement between a client and the person they hired for their opinion, and no triage taxonomy built for tickets handles it. Treating it as a defect ("we will investigate") is worse than useless, because it implies the finding was an error rather than a judgement. The second fact is that the deliverable's correctness is contested and frequently unfalsifiable in the timeframe. A recommendation is right or wrong over quarters, so satisfaction detaches entirely from outcome and attaches to the relationship, the clarity of the reasoning and whether the client felt heard. That makes sentiment, not resolution, the primary reading. Because of all this, consulting is the type where a support function is smallest and most likely to be an anti-pattern: routing a partner's client into a ticket queue is itself the failure. Support here mostly means keeping commitments and noticing relationships going wrong early, which is why the capabilities emphasised below are almost entirely relational.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | analysis, recommendation and advice, delivered by named senior people whose judgement is the product |
| pricing_shape | time and materials, day rate, or fixed fee per engagement — priced on the seniority of who does the thinking |
| margin_profile | highest gross margin in the service family and entirely dependent on utilisation of a small number of expensive people |
| post_sale_load | low in volume and high in seniority. Few contacts, each of which usually requires the person who did the original work |
| support_load | sparse, unpredictable and non-delegable. Contacts cluster around delivery of findings and around the moments the client tries to act on them |
| resolution_locus | a human rethinking, re-explaining or defending a judgement. There is no artefact to change and frequently nothing that can be called a fix |
| notes | The most useful question at intake is whether the contact is a misunderstanding, a disagreement or a scope request. All three arrive phrased identically and the correct responses are, respectively, explain, discuss, and price.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment`

Requires `trajectory`, `public_exposure`


> Sentiment is the primary reading in this type because outcome is unfalsifiable in the timeframe. A client who disagrees with a finding and is engaged is healthy; one who has stopped arguing has usually stopped listening, and the trajectory is the only thing that separates them.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `promised_at`, `due_at`, `owner_ref`


> With no artefact and no SLA, the commitment is very nearly the only objective obligation in the engagement. Missing one here is disproportionately damaging precisely because there is nothing else to be measured on.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `origin`, `escalation_owner_ref`


> Escalation in consulting is almost always partner-to-partner rather than tier-to-tier. The correct receiver is the person with the relationship, not the person with deeper technical expertise, and routing it as a technical escalation reads to the client as being handed off.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> Four deactivations makes this the thinnest branch in the library, and that is the honest reading rather than an unfinished one: consulting is the offering where a support function is least applicable, and a file that pretended otherwise would be inventing structure to look complete. The claim worth arguing with is deactivating knowledge_authoring — large firms do build genuine reusable methodology assets. The counterargument is that those are practice development, authored by the practice for its own consultants, and running them through a support knowledge programme mislabels who owns them.
